title: Hmong people
description: Ethnic group in southwest China and Southeast Asia
wiki_lead: The Hmong people (Hmong pronunciation: [m̥ɔ̃́]; RPA: Hmoob; Hmong Dô: Hmôngz; Nyiakeng Puachue Hmong: 𞄀𞄩𞄰; Pahawh Hmong: 𖬌𖬣𖬵; Chinese: 苗族蒙人) are an ethnic group from East and Southeast Asia. In China, the Hmong people are classified as a sub-group of the Miao people. The modern Hmong reside mainly in Southwestern China and Mainland Southeast Asian countries, such as Vietnam, Laos, Thailand, and Myanmar. There are also diaspora communities in the United States, Australia, France, and South America.
wiki_excerpt:
The Hmong people (Hmong pronunciation: [m̥ɔ̃́]; RPA: Hmoob; Hmong Dô: Hmôngz; Nyiakeng Puachue Hmong: 𞄀𞄩𞄰; Pahawh Hmong: 𖬌𖬣𖬵; Chinese: 苗族蒙人) are an ethnic group from East and Southeast Asia. In China, the Hmong people are classified as a sub-group of the Miao people. The modern Hmong reside mainly in Southwestern China and Mainland Southeast Asian countries, such as Vietnam, Laos, Thailand, and Myanmar. There are also diaspora communities in the United States, Australia, France, and South America.


Etymology
The term Hmong is the English spelling of the Hmong people's native name. It is a singular and a plural noun similar to "Japanese" and "French". Very little is known about the Hmong people's native name, as it is not mentioned in Chinese historical records, in which the Hmong are identified as Miao. Its meaning is debatable, and its origin is uncertain, though it can be traced to several provinces in China. However, Hmong Americans and Hmong Laotians often associate it with 'free' or 'fate' (hmoov); it serves as a reminder to them of their history of fighting oppression.
Before the 1970s, the term Miao ('barbarians', 'wild', 'seedlings', or 'sons of the soil'), also spelled Meo, was used in reference to the Hmong. In the 1970s, Yang Dao, a Hmong-American scholar, who at the time was the head of the Human Resource Department of the Ministry of Planning in the Royal Lao Government of Kingdom of Laos, advocated for the term Hmong with the support of clan leaders and then-leader Vang Pao. Dao insisted that both Meo and Miao were unacceptable, as his people had always called themselves by the name "Hmong" (which he defined as "free men"). Surrounding countries began to use the term Hmong after the United States Department of State used it for immigration screening in Thailand's Ban Vinai Refugee Camp. In 1994, Vang Pobzeb registered the term Hmong with the United Nations, making it the proper term to identify the Hmong people internationally. Soon after, there was a political push from Hmong-American politicians and activists to replace the term Miao with the term Hmong in China with little to no success.


Relationship to the Miao


Historical Miao
Historically, the term "Hmong" is not featured in any Chinese text, only the term "Miao". However it is uncertain if all mentions of Miao people referred to the Hmong people. According to Ruey (1962), the way in which Miao was used in Chinese can roughly be divided into three periods: a legendary period from 2300 BC to 200 BC, then a period when the term generally referred to southern barbarians until 1200 AD, and then a modern period during which the Hmong were probably included. Although the term appeared before the Qin dynasty (221 BC), throughout history Miao was used as a loose and general term by the Han to refer to southern barbarians. Only since the Tang dynasty did more evidence of its association with the Hmong become more apparent. In the 20th century, Western missionaries called the Hmong and Hmao the "Big Flowery Miao" (Da Hua Miao) and the "Little Flowery Miao" (Xiao Hua Miao). Another source states that the Green and White Miao were the Hmong, the Flowery Miao were the Hmao, the Black Miao were the Hmu, and the Red Miao were the Xong. According to She Miaojun, the Miao only existed as an exonym in the imagination of outsiders all the way up to the Qing dynasty. It did not refer to any self-defined ethnic group united by either territory or language. Others believe that Miao identity emerged during the rebellions of the 18th and 19th centuries.


Miao nationality
Today, the Hmong in China are categorized under the umbrella term Miáo (苗) along with three other indigenous cultural groups, which include non-Hmong peoples such as the Hmu and the Xong of southeast Guizhou. grok_lead: The Hmong people are an ethnic group originating from the mountainous highlands of southern China and Southeast Asia, including Laos, Vietnam, and Thailand, where they traditionally practiced slash-and-burn agriculture and maintained clan-based societies. Their languages belong to the Hmong-Mien family, with dialects varying by subgroup, and they have preserved oral traditions and shamanistic beliefs centered on ancestral spirits despite pressures from dominant cultures. Tracing their roots to ancient East Asia near the Yellow and Yangtze rivers around 4,000â3,000 BCE, the Hmong migrated southward over centuries, fleeing persecution and seeking autonomy in remote terrains, a pattern culminating in 19th-century movements into Indochina. During the Vietnam War era, Hmong irregular forces under leaders like Vang Pao fought alongside U.S. and allied troops in Laos ' "Secret War" against North Vietnamese and Pathet Lao communists, suffering heavy casualties that led to reprisals and mass exodus after 1975. This conflict prompted refugee flows to Thailand camps and subsequent resettlement, establishing vibrant diaspora communities in the United Statesâwhere over 300,000 Hmong Americans now reside, comprising about 1% of the U.S. Asian populationâthe French Guiana, Australia, and Canada, where they have adapted while sustaining cultural practices like elaborate embroidery, New Year festivals, and animal-sacrifice rituals for healing and rites of passage. Notable for their resilience in preserving identity amid historical marginalization, the Hmong exemplify adaptive highland societies whose empirical survival strategies prioritized mobility, kinship solidarity, and spiritual mediation over centralized authority.
